title: Symmetry as a route to generalized bosonic Kitaev chains
authors: Gideon Lee, Tony Jin, Aashish A. Clerk
abstract: The bosonic Kitaev chain (BKC) model is a deceptively simple looking quadratic pairing Hamiltonian. Despite being purely Hermitian, it exhibits a number of striking non-Hermitian topological phenomena, including skin effects. We show here how symmetries play a key role in this model, and how identifying these allows one to develop generalized BKC-like models. We emphasize the surprising fact that any quadratic bosonic pairing Hamiltonian with a sublattice (chiral) symmetry necessarily has a dynamical matrix with an effective time reversal symmetry. This symmetry is unrelated to physical time-reversal, but enables non-trivial topological invariants. We also discuss how this symmetry is unrelated to another key property of the BKC, the decoupling of quadrature dynamics. This feature can instead be connected to a distinct symmetry, namely an effective particle-hole symmetry of the dynamical matrix. We discuss non-trivial generalized BKC models that only keep one of these two effective symmetries intact. We also provide a classification of all translationally-invariant 1D pairing Hamiltonians, and show connections between the BKC and a well-studied non-Hermitian fermionic system, the symplectic Hatano-Nelson model.
summary: This work analyzes the symmetries governing the Bosonic Kitaev Chain and related quadratic pairing Hamiltonians. It demonstrates that two distinct types of effective symmetries—sublattice symmetry and particle-hole symmetry—govern different topological features like skin effects. The findings provide a comprehensive classification scheme for these 1D bosonic systems, extending to interacting models via mean-field theory.
main_problem: The paper investigates how symmetries dictate non-trivial topological phenomena, such as skin effects, in bosonic pairing Hamiltonians beyond the basic Kitaev model.
main_result: It establishes that two distinct symmetries—sublattice (chiral) symmetry and effective particle-hole symmetry from quadrature decoupling—can independently be used to construct generalized, stable bosonic pairing models with non-trivial topology.
method: The analysis relies on deriving the dynamics via a dynamical matrix in the quadrature basis and applying topological diagnostics like winding numbers or specialized invariants for bosonic systems.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Bosonic Kitaev Chain (BKC), a quadratic pairing Hamiltonian for bosons. The study extends to general 1D translationally-invariant quadratic bosonic Hamiltonians, including interactions treated at mean-field level.
key_observables: Non-Hermitian Skin Effect (NHSE), topological invariants derived from symmetries, and the spectral stability of the system's dynamical matrix eigenvalues.
important_parameters: Hopping ($w$), pairing ($\Delta$), interaction strengths ($U$, $g$), and momentum ($k$).
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximations (e.g., leading order in 1/N) or mean-field treatments when considering interacting terms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the BKC and highlights the two key symmetries: quadrature decoupling linked to particle-hole symmetry, and sublattice symmetry linked to an effective time-reversal symmetry.
paper_structure: The paper first analyzes the basic BKC model by identifying its inherent symmetries. It then develops generalized models based on preserving only one of these symmetries. The structure progresses through classifying all 1D quadratic systems and finally discusses extending the framework to interacting, non-quadratic Hamiltonians using mean-field theory.
why_interesting: The detailed symmetry analysis provides a powerful theoretical toolkit for understanding topological phases in bosonic quantum systems, which is crucial for designing novel superconducting or cavity QED circuits.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Left: Schematic of the bosonic Kitaev chain (BKC), a one-dimensional model with hopping iw and pairing i∆on each bond. Despite being Hermitian, it exhibits a number of striking features typically associated with non-Hermitian topology. Right: Two symmetries of the BKC relevant to its exceptional behaviour: decoupling of q and p quadrature dynamics (which can be mapped to a particle hole type sym- metry), and a sublattice or chiral symmetry (which becomes an effective time-reversal symmetry). More general BKC-like models can be constructed by retaining one or both of these symmetries.

Figure 2. Plot of the maximum imaginary part of any eigen- value of (a) ∆2-BKC, (b) ∆3-BKC, against the value of ∆2,3, and (c) g2-BKC, (d) g3-BKC, against the value of g1,2. The other (underlying bare BKC) parameters are set to w = 1, ∆= 0.25, and all values are computed under OBC for a range of system sizes L = 20, 40, 60, 80. The perturba- tions depicted in the left column break sublattice symmetry; accordingly the BKC under OBC is immediately unstable against such perturbations. Conversely, the perturbations depicted in the right column preserve sublattice symmetry; accordingly the stability of BKC under OBC is protected against such perturbations.
